query: For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the onset or suppression of corrosion-related degradation in harsh environments at room and elevated temperatures? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to the untreated reference, applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: Controlling pre-exposure surface oxide formation on Q235 carbon steel through thermal oxidation treatments produces an adherent, protective film (primarily Fe3O4 or Fe2O3) that inhibits the ingress of corrosive species at room temperature, while elevated temperatures may lead to thermal-induced film degradation and localized corrosion development.
generation.material_initial_state: As-received Q235 carbon steel with its native microstructure and composition.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to controlled thermal oxidation treatments in dry air at temperatures ranging from 150 °C to 300 °C for varying durations to engineer the surface oxide characteristics.
generation.conditions: Expose both treated and untreated samples to a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution under two temperature regimes: room temperature and an elevated temperature (approximately 70–100 °C) with controlled humidity and oxygen availability.
generation.structural_mediator: The nature, thickness, and adhesion of the iron oxide layers formed on the steel surface that serve as the physical barrier against corrosive species.
generation.mechanism: The pre-formed, adherent oxide film acts as a physical barrier that limits the diffusion of Cl⁻, O₂, and H₂O into the underlying metal. At room temperature, the film remains coherent and effective; however, at elevated temperatures, thermal expansion and stress may induce spallation or microcracking in the film, compromising its integrity and leading to accelerated localized corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Optimally treated samples are expected to exhibit a lower corrosion rate—as evidenced by reduced weight loss and higher impedance measurements—compared to untreated references under both conditions. A decisive falsification would occur if the treated samples show similar or higher corrosion rates under both temperature regimes.
generation.baseline: Untreated Q235 steel exposed under identical corrosive conditions.
generation.boundary: The study is conducted in well-controlled laboratory environments with fixed chloride concentration, humidity, and oxygen levels. Variations outside these conditions or at temperatures significantly higher than the tested range may result in different oxidation behaviors.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainties remain regarding the precise temperature threshold at which thermal-induced oxide film degradation initiates, and the quantitative kinetics of film spallation versus protective performance over extended exposure periods.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Q235 steel samples, one undergoing controlled thermal oxidation (pre-oxidation treatment) and one left untreated. Expose both sets to a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution under room temperature and elevated temperature (70–100 °C) conditions. Monitor surface film integrity, weight loss, and perform electrochemical impedance spectroscopy over defined intervals.
measurements: Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) to assess film morphology and spallation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the pre-oxidized samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in corrosion rate or improved impedance compared to the untreated controls at room temperature, or if the treated samples do not exhibit the expected film degradation (spallation or localized cracks) at elevated temperatures.

The full spectrum (Figure 10a) indicates the presence of Ti, Nb, Sn, Mo, C, and O elements in the oxide film/passivation layer on CR75. The presence of C and O elemental peaks in the full spectrum result from surface carbon contamination and the oxide layer. Narrow scans of the O 1s, Ti 2p, Nb 3d, Sn 3d, and Mo 3d elements of the CR75 sample are shown in Figure 10b–f, respectively. The O 1s peaks correspond to the OH−, O−, and O2− oxidation states; the Ti 2p peaks belong to the Ti4+ oxidation state; the Nb 3d peaks are related to the Nb5+ oxidation state; the Sn 3d spectrums are ascribed to the Sn0 and Sn4+ oxidation states; and the Mo 3d peaks are composed of the Mo0, Mo2+, Mo4+, and Mo6+ oxidation states. Therefore, the surface oxide film/passivation layer of the CR75 mainly comprises TiO2, Nb2O5, SnO2, MoO, MoO2, and MoO3. The presence of Nb2O5 improves the resistance to Cl− ion erosion and enhances the structural integrity of the oxide film/passivation layer []. (1) The (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating was prepared by plasma spraying on substrate of the Q235 steel, consisting of a simple FCC solid solution with Laves phase, and the coating bonded well to the substrate. (2) Elemental segregation occurred between the dendrites and the interdendrites of the coating, and the elements Cr and Nb with high melting point were enriched between the interdendrites. This phenomenon may be due to the difference in melting point of the element and the characteristics of the plasma spraying process. (3) The coating has a microhardness of 321 HV0.5, which can effectively improve the surface hardness of the Q235 steel part. (4) The (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating exhibited excellent corrosion resistance in the electrochemical corrosion test of a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution comparing to previously studied coatings prepared by other processes. (5) In the 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution, the selective corrosion occurred on the surface of (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating, while the interdendritic phase rich in Nb and Cr was preferentially corroded as an anode, and the dendritic phase rich in Co, Ni, and Fe was protected as a cathode.

In this paper, the CoCrFeNiTix HEA coatings are prepared on Q235 steel substrate by laser cladding. The effect of Ti content on the microstructure and corrosion resistance in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution was studied. Furthermore, the corrosion resistance mechanism was analyzed experimentally and by first-principles calculations.

proposals.intervention: Induce and control the formation of specific surface oxide films via controlled pre-oxidation treatments (e.g., thermal oxidation in dry air at 150–300 °C for varying durations)
proposals.conditions: Expose treated and untreated samples to harsh corrosive environments (e.g., 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution) at room temperature and at an elevated temperature (≈70–100 °C) under controlled humidity and oxygen availability
proposals.structural_mediator: The nature, thickness, and adhesion of the iron oxide layers (e.g., formation of magnetite Fe3O4 or hematite Fe2O3) on the steel surface
proposals.mechanism: A pre-formed, adherent oxide film acts as a physical barrier to inhibit the ingress of corrosive species (Cl⁻, O₂, and H₂O). At room temperature the film remains compact and protective, whereas at elevated temperatures, thermal stresses may compromise its integrity. The study will test the hypothesis that controlled pre-oxidation can either delay the onset of film breakdown at higher temperatures or, if improperly formed, accelerate localized corrosion via film spallation.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Samples with an optimally developed oxide film will exhibit lower corrosion rates (as measured by weight loss and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy) compared to untreated references at both temperature regimes. A decisive falsification would be if controlled oxide films either do not reduce or worsen corrosion relative to the reference under both conditions.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: It isolates the effect of surface film characteristics on corrosion degradation by comparing purposely modified surfaces against untreated Q235 steel, under identical environmental exposures at varying temperatures.

proposals.material_system: Q235 carbon steel with controlled microstructural states
proposals.intervention: Implement tailored short-term annealing treatments at varied temperatures (e.g., 600 °C for 1 hour versus 800 °C for 1 hour) to modify grain size and impurity (e.g., sulfur or phosphorus) segregation at grain boundaries
proposals.conditions: Expose microstructure-modified samples and untreated Q235 steel to a corrosive environment (3.5 wt.% NaCl solution) at room temperature and a moderately elevated temperature (≈80 °C) in a laboratory-controlled electrochemical cell
proposals.structural_mediator: The distribution and concentration of impurity elements at grain boundaries as well as grain size effects, which can govern localized corrosion pit formation
proposals.mechanism: Grain boundaries can act as preferential sites for corrosion pit initiation due to impurity segregation. The hypothesis is that a controlled coarsening (or refinement) coupled with reduced impurity segregation at grain boundaries could lead to suppressed localized corrosion. Monitoring electrochemical responses (potentiodynamic polarization) would test if reduced grain boundary reactivity correlates with improved corrosion resistance.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Samples treated to minimize impurity segregation at grain boundaries should show a higher corrosion potential and lower pit density compared to the untreated reference. A decisive falsification would be if no significant difference in corrosion initiation (or an opposite trend) is observed between the modified and unmodified microstructures.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: It probes the mechanistic role of microstructural features—specifically grain boundary chemistry—in the onset of corrosion degradation and how their modification can suppress the phenomenon under different thermal conditions.

proposals.material_system: Q235 carbon steel subjected to controlled cathodic polarization
proposals.intervention: Apply a cathodic polarization treatment under controlled current density conditions to promote in situ hydrogen charging (or, alternately, use hydrogen inhibitors) prior to corrosion exposure
proposals.conditions: Test the hydrogen-charged versus non-charged (or inhibitor-treated) samples in a corrosive electrolyte (e.g., 3.5 wt.% NaCl) at both room temperature and at an elevated temperature (≈60–80 °C) in deaerated conditions to isolate hydrogen effects
proposals.structural_mediator: The accumulation of hydrogen at dislocations and within the steel matrix which may lead to microstructural embrittlement or localized corrosion via hydrogen-induced cracking
proposals.mechanism: The hypothesis is that hydrogen absorption during cathodic polarization modifies the near-surface microstructure, promoting embrittlement and localized corrosion crack initiation. Using inhibitors to prevent hydrogen uptake should conversely suppress these corrosion-related mechanisms. The study isolates the effect of hydrogen by comparing samples with and without hydrogen exposure under identical corrosive conditions.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Hydrogen-charged samples will show enhanced localized corrosion damage, reduced ductility, and increased cracking relative to untreated references; if hydrogen inhibitors are applied, these degradative features should be significantly suppressed. A decisive falsification would be the absence of any correlation between hydrogen charging and increased corrosion damage.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: It targets the role of hydrogen (induced or inhibited) in corrosion degradation, providing a mechanistic explanation that is testable by isolating hydrogen uptake as the governing cause, across different temperature regimes.

proposals.material_system: Q235 carbon steel with surface modification via low-alloy additions
proposals.intervention: Perform localized surface alloying via laser surface treatment to introduce minor elements (e.g., Mo or Cr) that favor the formation of more stable, protective oxides on the steel surface
proposals.conditions: Expose laser-alloyed surfaces and non-treated Q235 steel to cyclic corrosion tests in a salt fog chamber, under both room temperature and elevated temperatures (≈80 °C), ensuring similar exposure time and humidity conditions
proposals.structural_mediator: The formation of a modified surface layer enriched in Mo or Cr that alters the oxide scale composition and improves its structural integrity and adhesion
proposals.mechanism: The hypothesis is that the introduction of alloying elements via laser surface treatment alters the oxidation kinetics and stability of the passive film. At room temperature, these elements facilitate the formation of a dense, adherent oxide, but at elevated temperatures, the altered composition maintains its protective nature by resisting spallation and excessive dissolution. This mechanistic study isolates the effect of chemical composition at the surface on the corrosion behavior.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Laser-alloyed surfaces will exhibit increased corrosion resistance, demonstrated by lower mass loss and fewer surface defects compared to untreated surfaces under both temperature regimes. The decisive falsification would occur if the modified surfaces do not show any meaningful improvement or if they exhibit accelerated degradation relative to the reference.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: It examines a surface engineering approach that directly tests the role of surface chemical composition and oxide phase stability in controlling corrosion-related degradation, under carefully controlled harsh environmental conditions.

decision.rationale: Direction A directly addresses the question by isolating the role of surface oxide films on Q235 steel. It tests whether controlled pre-oxidation creates a protective barrier that suppresses corrosion at room temperature and how thermal stresses at elevated temperatures compromise film integrity, leading to accelerated degradation. This approach maintains the pre-exposure state of Q235 steel and uses well-established mechanisms, while the potential issue of film spallation at high temperatures is explicitly addressed in the hypothesis.
